pages.text: Every Thursday evening in Asafo, the prepaid electricity meter on the compound-house wall began its sharp warning beep—credit almost finished again. Tenants blamed one another around the courtyard. Uncle Nii lowered his voice: “A man at the lorry park offered to connect our heavy sockets so that they bypass the meter, for a small fee, so our credits stop draining.” Mansa exchanged a worried look with her cousin Tetteh. “Before anyone touches illegal wires, Uncle,” Mansa asked respectfully, “may Tetteh and I calculate where the kilowatt-hours are actually going?”

Tenants blamed one another around the courtyard.

Uncle Nii lowered his voice: “A man at the lorry park offered to connect our heavy sockets so that they bypass the meter, for a small fee, so our credits stop draining.” Mansa exchanged a worried look with her cousin Tetteh.
“Before anyone touches illegal wires, Uncle,” Mansa asked respectfully, “may Tetteh and I calculate where the kilowatt-hours are actually going?”
pages.alt: In a Ghanaian compound-house courtyard at dusk, tenants gather anxiously beneath a wall-mounted prepaid electricity meter flashing a red low-credit light while Mansa holds up her science notebook.

pages.text: Mansa and Tetteh read the rating plate on every appliance—never touching live wires—and recorded each power rating in watts (W). “Electrical power is voltage multiplied by current: P = V × I,” Tetteh said. “But the meter charges us for energy. Energy is power in kilowatts multiplied by time in hours, E = P × t, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh).” They began to calculate. The compound’s ten old 60-watt filament bulbs, burning five hours a night, used 3.0 kWh; ten 9-watt LEDs would need only 0.45 kWh. The 1,500-watt pressing iron, used for two hours, took another 3.0 kWh. And Auntie Akweley’s secondhand refrigerator had a torn rubber door seal, so its 300-watt compressor ran non-stop, day and night.

pages.alt: Mansa and Tetteh inspecting the metal wattage rating label on the back of an unplugged pressing iron and checking a torn rubber door gasket on an old refrigerator, recording figures in a table.

pages.text: On Saturday, licensed electrician Master Owusu came to inspect the courtyard wiring. He praised the audit, then pointed to a sharper danger. Three tenants had plugged a kettle, a hotplate, and a television into one cheap extension board. Its plastic casing had turned brown and brittle. “Too much current through a thin cable makes it heat up until the insulation melts,” he warned. “A proper circuit breaker or fuse cuts the current before that happens. An illegal bypass is often done with the wrong cable, and it can leave the wiring without that protection. That is how compound-house fires and fatal electric shocks start.”

pages.text: Tetteh shared what the class had learned in Social Studies. “Uncle Nii, please, stolen power is not free,” he said gently. “When people bypass meters, the power company loses the money it needs to maintain transformers and cables. Unmetered loads can also overload a local transformer until it trips, and then the whole neighbourhood sits in darkness. Honest customers can end up paying higher tariffs to cover the losses. And tampering with a meter is a criminal offence in Ghana.”

pages.text: Uncle Nii rubbed his chin. Auntie Akweley spoke quietly. “Whether in church, at the mosque, or by family custom, taking what you have not paid for is theft—even when the wire is hidden inside the wall. My Muslim neighbours call it a breach of amanah, trust. My pastor says integrity means doing right in secret just as in public. And our elders say a good name is better than riches.” Uncle Nii took out his phone and deleted the wireman’s number on the spot.

pages.text: Together, the tenants replaced the torn refrigerator gasket so cold air stopped escaping. They swapped the old filament bulbs for 9-watt LEDs, reduced ironing from two hours each day to one three-hour session per week, and threw out the scorched extension board. Two weeks later, their prepaid credit lasted nearly twice as long—legally and safely. Pinning the wattage chart on the veranda wall, Mansa smiled. “Physics showed us the leak, civic duty protects our transformer, and honesty lets every room sleep safely.”

activities.question: A 2,000 W (2 kW) electric kettle boils water for a total of 0.5 hours across a day. How much electrical energy does it consume?
Why does plugging high-wattage appliances like a hotplate and kettle into one thin extension cord create a severe fire risk?
options: Together they draw large current that overheats cables and melts insulation
Voltage disappears completely whenever two plugs share a socket
LED bulbs send cold air back down the extension cable

activities.question: How does illegal meter bypassing harm the wider Ghanaian community?
options: It lowers the wattage rating of old refrigerators
It increases hydro dam water levels at Akosombo automatically
It can overload transformers, create fire hazards, and hurt power supply

activities.question: Apply it: A shop runs a 100 W fan for 10 hours and a 1,000 W heater for 30 minutes. Which uses more energy?
options: The heater, because its power rating is higher
They use exactly the same energy
The fan: 1.0 kWh against 0.5 kWh for the heater

activities.prompt: Put the compound house’s problem-solving journey in chronological order.
items: Rapidly draining prepaid credits tempt a tenant to consider a meter bypass.
Mansa and Tetteh audit appliance wattages and hours to calculate kWh used.
Master Owusu shows how overloaded extension sockets create fire hazards.
Tenants mend the fridge seal, batch-iron clothes, and switch to LED bulbs.

activities.definition: A unit of electrical energy equal to one kilowatt (1,000 watts) of power used steadily for one hour.
distractors: The speed at which electrons travel through a copper wire in one second
A safety switch that melts when current becomes too small

glossary.definition: The rate at which electrical energy is transferred by an appliance, measured in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW), where P = V × I.
An instrument measuring total electrical energy consumed in kilowatt-hours (kWh).
An automatic safety switch designed to cut off electrical current when an overload or short circuit occurs.
The official schedule of rates or prices charged per unit for public utilities such as electricity or water.
Steadfast honesty and adherence to moral principles even when wrongdoing could be hidden from authorities.
